transcript.content: Hello. What brings you into the clinic today?

When I have to sit and focus on these long claim files at work, my mind just checks out and I end up putting them off or staring at the screen instead of getting them done. It's really starting to hurt my performance, and I just can't seem to get through them.
Have you struggled with these types of focus and attention issues since childhood, or is this a relatively new problem for you?

It actually goes back to childhood, because even in elementary school, my teachers noted that I daydreamed a lot and constantly lost worksheets or forgot to turn in homework. However, it only became a severe, disruptive problem over the last year and a few months when the workload at my job changed.
Over the past year, since your work struggles worsened, have you also been feeling persistently down, sad, or lost interest in things you normally enjoy?

No, I haven't really felt persistently down or lost interest in the things I like to do. I do feel incredibly stressed and anxious about my job security because of my struggles at work, but it's more about the pressure than feeling depressed.

Is this anxiety and worry mostly focused on your job security and work performance, or do you find yourself worrying excessively about many different areas of your life, such as health, family, or everyday minor tasks?

It's definitely focused on my job security and work performance, not other areas of my life. I'm constantly anxious that I'm going to get fired because of my high error rates, unfinished files, and the two write-ups I've already received. My family and health are fine, but the fear of losing my job is what is really stressing me out.

Do you find that these difficulties with attention, organization, or forgetfulness also cause problems in your daily life outside of work, such as with household chores, paying bills, or keeping track of your personal belongings?

I haven't really noticed these issues affecting things like my chores or paying bills. However, I do sometimes forget personal commitments, like missing a couple of dentist appointments because I got wrapped up in something else and it slipped my mind. For the most part, though, the struggle is really centered around my work.

Before this workload change a year ago, how did you manage in previous jobs or during your school years? Did you experience similar, even if milder, difficulties with focus and organization in those environments?

In high school and community college, I got by by cramming right before exams and relying on my memory for big-picture concepts, so my tendency to drift off or lose things didn't cause too much trouble. But looking further back to elementary school, I definitely had similar issues; teachers often noted on my report cards that I daydreamed a lot and constantly lost my homework or worksheets.
Did your feelings of intense stress and anxiety about your job security start within three months of that workload change a year ago?

I'm not entirely sure if it started within that exact three-month window. The stress and anxiety really built up gradually over time as I realized I couldn't keep up with the new system and started getting negative feedback from my supervisor.
Do you find it difficult to focus, listen, or stay organized in other areas of your life outside of work, such as during conversations, while reading, or when trying to relax?

I haven't really noticed those issues as much during conversations or when I'm trying to relax. I mostly notice them when I'm trying to handle my work tasks, organize my messy desk, or remember appointments.
Do you often find yourself fidgeting, feeling physically restless, or having trouble staying seated when you are expected to?

Yes, when I'm sitting at my desk, I constantly bounce my leg, click my pen, or shift around because I feel really restless if I try to stop. During long team meetings, I also find myself getting up to grab water or use the restroom even when I don't actually need to, just because I feel too antsy to stay seated.

final_diagnosis.reason: The patient meets the diagnostic criteria for Attention-Deficit Hyperactivity Disorder (ADHD), combined presentation, represented by ICD-10 code F90.0. The patient reports a childhood history of inattention (daydreaming, losing worksheets, forgetting homework) that has persisted into adulthood and currently causes severe impairment at work (high error rates, unfinished files, write-ups) and some impairment in personal life (forgetting appointments, messy desk). Symptoms of hyperactivity/impulsivity are also present, including physical restlessness, fidgeting (leg bouncing, pen clicking), and difficulty remaining seated during long meetings. These symptoms are not better explained by Generalized Anxiety Disorder (F41.1) or an Adjustment Disorder (F43.2), as the patient's anxiety is situational and secondary to their ADHD-related work struggles, and the core ADHD symptoms have been present since childhood.
